dialogue.en: Where Do I Belong? Third Culture Kids

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today's question sounds simple: where are you from? My guest, Dr Sara Kareem, finds it surprisingly hard to answer.
That's right. I was born in Baghdad, grew up in Dubai and studied in Manchester. So when someone asks me where I'm from, I usually hesitate.
You describe yourself as a "third culture kid". What does that mean?
The term was coined by the sociologist Ruth Hill Useem in the 1950s. It describes children who spend a large part of their formative years outside their parents' culture.
They build a "third culture": a mix of their parents' culture and the cultures they live in.
Is that a gift or a problem?
Honestly, both. Third culture kids tend to be adaptable, multilingual and good at reading people. But many of them also describe a feeling of rootlessness.
Because they don't fully belong anywhere?
Exactly. They often feel more at home with other people who have moved around than with people from their own passport country.
What would you say to a young person who feels like that?
I'd say that belonging doesn't have to be about one place. It can be about people, values or even a language. Home can be plural.

reading.en: The Myth of a Single Identity
reading.text: Ask a stranger who they are, and the answer will usually come in a single word: a nationality, a profession, perhaps a religion. Yet each of us carries many identities at once. The same woman may be an Iraqi, a doctor, a mother, a football fan, a poet and a speaker of three languages. Which of these matters most depends on where she is and who she is talking to. In a hospital, she is first a doctor; at a stadium, she is simply a fan. The economist and philosopher Amartya Sen argued in his book Identity and Violence that reducing people to one identity is not only inaccurate but dangerous. When a community is persuaded that only one label truly defines its members, it becomes easier to divide the world into "us" and "them". Psychology helps to explain why such divisions form so easily. In the early 1970s, the social psychologist Henri Tajfel divided volunteers into groups on the most trivial basis imaginable, such as which of two abstract painters they preferred. Even though the groups were meaningless, and the volunteers never met the other members, they still tended to give more rewards to people in their own group. If a preference for a painter can create loyalty, it is hardly surprising that language, nationality or religion can create much stronger bonds. None of this means that belonging is harmful. On the contrary, a sense of belonging is linked to better mental health and greater resilience. The problem begins only when one identity is allowed to swallow all the others. Recognising our plural identities, Sen suggested, is not a weakness but a defence: it reminds us that the person on the other side of a dividing line usually shares far more with us than a single label would suggest.

lines.s: Welcome back to The Thinking Room. Why is it that we forget a new phone number in minutes but remember a song from childhood? Professor Hadi Nouri studies memory. Welcome.
Thank you. The first person to study forgetting scientifically was a German psychologist, Hermann Ebbinghaus, back in 1885.
What did he do?
He memorised lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself at different intervals. He found that most of the forgetting happens very quickly, within the first day.
That's depressing!
It is, but he also found the solution: every time you review the information, the forgetting curve becomes flatter. That's the idea behind spaced repetition.
So cramming the night before an exam is a bad idea?

It might help you pass tomorrow, but you'll lose most of it within weeks. And there's another factor people ignore: sleep. During deep sleep, the brain replays and consolidates what you learned during the day.
So the best study tip is to go to bed?
Almost! Review a little, test yourself, then sleep. What you remember a month later is what really counts.

reading.text: Most of us imagine memory as a kind of video recorder: we experience an event, the brain stores it, and later we simply press "play". Decades of research suggest that this picture is wrong. Every time we recall an event, we do not replay it; we rebuild it, and each reconstruction can introduce small changes. In a famous experiment in 1974, the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed volunteers films of car accidents and then asked how fast the cars were going. The only difference between the groups was a single verb. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other gave higher estimates than those who heard the word "hit". A week later, more people in the "smashed" group claimed to have seen broken glass, even though there was none in the film. Loftus later went further. In the 1990s, she and her colleagues showed that it was possible to plant an entirely false memory. Participants were given short descriptions of childhood events, supposedly provided by their relatives. One of the events, being lost in a shopping centre as a child, had never happened. Nevertheless, around a quarter of the participants came to remember it, at least in part, and some even added details of their own. Such findings have serious consequences. Courts have traditionally treated a confident eyewitness as powerful evidence, yet confidence and accuracy are not the same thing. Researchers now recommend that police interview witnesses as early as possible and avoid leading questions. For the rest of us, the lesson is humbling. The memories we feel most certain about are not necessarily the most accurate ones. What we remember is less a record of the past than a story we keep retelling, and, like all stories, it changes a little each time it is told.

lines.s: Welcome back to The Thinking Room. They say a lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes. Is that actually true? Dr Omar Saleh studies online behaviour.
Unfortunately, the data suggests it is. In 2018, researchers at MIT published a huge study of stories shared on Twitter over more than ten years.
What did they find?
False stories spread further, faster and deeper than true ones. On average, a false story was about seventy per cent more likely to be retweeted than a true one.
Was that because of bots?
That's what everyone assumed, but no. The bots spread true and false stories at roughly the same rate. It was humans who made the difference.
So why do we prefer false stories?
Mainly because they're new and surprising. False stories tend to make people feel shock or disgust, and we love being the first to share something shocking. It makes us look well-informed.
What can listeners do about it?
Pause before you press "share". If a story makes you very angry or very excited, that's exactly the moment to check it.

reading.text: In 1971, long before the first smartphone, the economist Herbert Simon made a remarkable prediction. A wealth of information, he wrote, creates a poverty of attention. Half a century later, his words describe the business model of the world's most powerful technology companies. Most social media platforms are free to use, but they are not charities. They earn their money by selling advertisers access to our attention, and the longer we stay on their apps, the more money they make. This is what critics call the attention economy. To keep us scrolling, platforms rely on algorithms that learn what we react to and show us more of it. The problem is that what we react to most strongly is not always what is good for us. A study published in 2017 analysed hundreds of thousands of posts about controversial topics and found that every moral or emotional word, such as "shame", "evil" or "attack", increased the number of times a post was shared by about twenty per cent. In other words, the system tends to reward outrage. Defenders of the platforms reject this picture. They argue that users are not helpless victims and that algorithms simply give people what they ask for. They also point out that social media has given a voice to millions of people who were previously ignored, from small business owners to activists in remote areas. Both arguments contain some truth. What seems clear is that attention has become one of the most valuable resources of our age, and that we rarely notice when it is taken from us. The first step towards protecting it may be surprisingly simple: recognising that every notification, autoplay video and endless feed has been carefully designed to compete for the few hours we have each day.

dialogue.en: Will a Robot Take My Job?

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today's question keeps many listeners awake at night: will a robot take my job? I'm joined by the economist Dr Rana Haddad.
Thanks for having me. It's a question people have been asking for two hundred years, since workers in England first smashed textile machines.
But isn't this time different, with artificial intelligence?
In some ways, yes. In 2013, two Oxford researchers estimated that around forty-seven per cent of American jobs were at high risk of automation. That figure caused a lot of panic.
Were they right?

Later studies were more cautious. The OECD looked at tasks rather than whole jobs and concluded that about fourteen per cent of jobs were at high risk, while another thirty-two per cent would change significantly.
So most jobs won't disappear, but they will change.
Exactly. Machines are good at routine, predictable tasks. They're much worse at creativity, empathy and dealing with the unexpected.
What's your advice for young people?

Don't try to compete with machines at what they do best. Focus on the skills they find hardest: communication, judgement and the ability to keep learning. Given that the average career may now last fifty years, you'll probably need to reskill more than once.

reading.en: Is the Five-Day Week Out of Date?
reading.ar: هل أصبح أسبوع الأيام الخمسة قديماً؟
reading.text: The five-day working week feels so natural that it is easy to forget it was once a radical idea. In 1926, the American car maker Henry Ford reduced his factory workers' week from six days to five without cutting their pay. Critics predicted disaster, but Ford was convinced that rested workers would be more productive, and that people with free time would spend more money on goods such as cars. Four years later, the economist John Maynard Keynes went much further. In a famous essay, he predicted that by around 2030, thanks to technology, people in rich countries might need to work only fifteen hours a week. With that date now approaching, his prediction looks wildly optimistic. Productivity has risen enormously, yet most full-time employees still work around forty hours. Recently, however, the idea of a shorter week has returned. In 2022, sixty-one companies in the United Kingdom, employing almost three thousand people, took part in a six-month trial of a four-day week with no loss of pay. By the end of the trial, the vast majority of the companies had decided to continue, and several made the change permanent. Employees reported less stress and fewer sick days, while revenue at most companies stayed roughly the same. Sceptics urge caution. The companies in the trial chose to take part, so they may have been unusually suited to the experiment. A four-day week is also far easier to introduce in an office than in a hospital, a school or a restaurant, where someone must be present every day. Nevertheless, the experiment raises an important question. Given that machines can now do so much of our work, should the benefits come in the form of higher profits, or more time? Were Keynes alive today, he would probably be asking the same thing.

lines.s: Welcome back to The Thinking Room. Everyone complains about prices, but few of us understand inflation. Dr Yusuf Ali, an economist, is here to explain.

Happy to help. Inflation simply means that, over time, the same amount of money buys less. If a sandwich cost two thousand dinars last year and costs two thousand two hundred today, prices have risen by ten per cent.
Why does it happen?

There are two classic causes. Sometimes people have more money to spend than there are goods to buy, so prices are pulled up. Other times, the cost of producing things rises, for example when oil becomes more expensive, so prices are pushed up.
Is a little inflation bad?
Not necessarily. Most central banks actually aim for about two per cent a year. A small, steady rise encourages people to spend and invest rather than hoard cash.
And when it gets out of control?

Then you get hyperinflation. In Germany in 1923, people carried banknotes in wheelbarrows to buy bread. Much more recently, in 2009, Zimbabwe printed a one-hundred-trillion-dollar note, and it still wasn't enough for a bus ticket for long.
That's terrifying.
It is. Hyperinflation destroys people's savings and their trust in money itself. That trust, more than paper or gold, is what really gives money its value.

reading.text: It seems obvious that a country rich in oil, gas or minerals should also be a prosperous one. Yet economists have long noticed a puzzling pattern: many resource-rich countries grow more slowly, suffer more conflict and have weaker institutions than countries with few natural resources at all. In 1993, the British economist Richard Auty gave this pattern a name that stuck: the resource curse. Several explanations have been proposed. The first is economic. When a country starts exporting large amounts of a valuable resource, its currency tends to rise in value, which makes its other exports, such as crops or manufactured goods, more expensive abroad. Local farms and factories struggle to compete, and the economy becomes dangerously dependent on a single commodity. This effect is known as "Dutch disease", after the problems the Netherlands faced following the discovery of large natural gas fields in 1959. A second problem is volatility. Commodity prices can soar one year and plummet the next, so governments that rely on them face constant cycles of boom and bust. A third explanation is political. When a government earns most of its money from oil rather than from taxes, it has less need to listen to its citizens, and the temptation to use the wealth to reward supporters can be hard to resist. The curse, however, is not inevitable. Norway discovered oil in the late 1960s, yet it is now one of the wealthiest and most stable countries in the world. Instead of spending its oil revenue immediately, it saved much of it in a national fund, which is now worth more than a trillion dollars. Much as the situation differs from country to country, the lesson seems clear: natural wealth is not a guarantee of prosperity. What matters is not how much a country has under the ground, but how wisely it is managed above it.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Imagine being able to edit DNA as easily as you edit a document. That's the promise of a technology called CRISPR. Dr Maya Taha is a geneticist. Maya, what exactly is CRISPR?
Put simply, it's a pair of molecular scissors. Scientists can use it to find a specific section of DNA and cut it, remove it or replace it.
Where did it come from?

Ironically, from bacteria, which use it to defend themselves against viruses. In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed how it could be turned into a tool for editing genes. In 2020, they won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.
What can it do for patients?
It may well transform the treatment of inherited diseases. Some patients with serious blood disorders have already been treated successfully.
But there's a darker side, isn't there?
There is. In 2018, a Chinese scientist announced that he had edited the genes of twin baby girls. The scientific community was shocked, and he was later sentenced to three years in prison.
Why was it so controversial?

Because he edited embryos, so the changes could be passed on to future generations, and because nobody could be sure of the long-term effects. Most scientists agree that we should cure diseases, but very few think we're ready to redesign human beings.

reading.text: On 5 July 1996, at a research centre near Edinburgh in Scotland, a lamb was born who would soon become the most famous sheep in history. Her name was Dolly, and she was the first mammal ever cloned from an adult cell. Scientists had taken a cell from a six-year-old sheep and used it to create an embryo that was genetically identical to the original animal. It had taken 277 attempts to produce a single healthy lamb. When the news was announced the following year, the reaction was extraordinary. Newspapers predicted that human cloning was bound to follow within a few years. Politicians called for urgent laws, and ethicists warned that we were entering uncharted territory. Some imagined wealthy people cloning themselves; others feared armies of identical soldiers. Nearly three decades later, none of these predictions has come true. Dozens of countries have prohibited human reproductive cloning, and most scientists consider it both unsafe and unnecessary. Cloned animals often suffer from health problems, and Dolly herself died at the age of six, younger than most sheep of her kind. Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to conclude that Dolly changed nothing. The techniques developed to create her helped scientists understand how adult cells can be "reprogrammed", research that later led to new ways of producing stem cells without using human embryos. Today, cloning is used in agriculture, in medical research and, controversially, by companies that offer to clone people's pets for tens of thousands of dollars. Perhaps the most important lesson of Dolly is about prediction itself. The public debate focused almost entirely on dramatic scenarios that never happened, while the quieter, more useful consequences went largely unnoticed. When we discuss the ethics of new technologies such as gene editing, we may well be making the same mistake.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today we're asking a very old question: where do our ideas about justice come from? Professor Nadia Jaber is a legal historian.
Thank you. And as an Iraqi, I have to begin in Babylon. Around 1754 BC, King Hammurabi had nearly three hundred laws carved onto a tall black stone.
Why does that matter so much?
Because the laws were written down and displayed in public. For the first time, people could know the rules in advance. That's one of the foundations of the rule of law.
Weren't the punishments very harsh?

Many were, and they depended on your social class. But there are surprisingly modern ideas too. The very first law says that if you accuse someone of murder and cannot prove it, you will be punished yourself. In other words, the burden of proof is on the accuser.
And Magna Carta?

That's England, 1215. The barons forced King John to accept that even the king was subject to the law. One famous clause says that no free man may be imprisoned except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.
Where can people see Hammurabi's stone today?
Sadly, not in Iraq. The original is in the Louvre in Paris. But its message belongs to all of us: power should be limited by laws that everyone can read.

reading.text: Nearly two thousand years ago, the Roman poet Juvenal asked a question that still troubles political thinkers: who will guard the guardians themselves? Any society needs people with the power to make and enforce laws, but the more power they are given, the greater the danger that it will be misused. In 1887, the British historian Lord Acton expressed the same fear in a sentence that has been quoted ever since: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. One of the most influential answers to this problem was put forward by the French philosopher Montesquieu in 1748. In The Spirit of the Laws, he argued that liberty could only be protected if the power to make laws, the power to carry them out and the power to judge were held by separate institutions. If one person or group controlled all three, he warned, there would be no limit to what they could do. His ideas were adopted by the authors of the United States Constitution and have since influenced constitutions all over the world. Modern democracies have added further safeguards. A free press can expose wrongdoing that officials would prefer to keep hidden. Ombudsmen investigate complaints against public bodies, and independent courts can overturn decisions that break the law. Elections, meanwhile, allow citizens to remove leaders who have lost their trust. None of these institutions is perfect. Courts can be pressured, journalists can be silenced, and elections can be manipulated. History shows that checks and balances are rarely destroyed overnight; more often they are weakened gradually, one small change at a time, until it is too late to reverse the process. For this reason, many legal scholars argue that the final guardians of a free society are not judges or journalists, but ordinary citizens who understand their rights and are prepared to defend them.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Why do some speeches change history while others are forgotten in minutes? Our guest, Dr Hana Rashid, teaches public speaking.
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the best guide was written more than two thousand years ago. In his book on rhetoric, Aristotle described three ways to persuade an audience.
Which are?
Ethos, pathos and logos. Ethos is your credibility: why should people trust you? Pathos is emotion: do they care? And logos is logic: do your arguments make sense?
Which one matters most?
All three, but in the right order. If the audience doesn't trust you, your logic won't be heard. And facts alone rarely move people. A single personal story often does more than a page of statistics.
Isn't that a bit manipulative?

It can be. Demagogues use pathos without logos; they make people angry or afraid and give them no evidence. That's why a good listener should always ask: what is the speaker making me feel, and is there any proof behind it?
Any practical tips for listeners who have to give a speech?
Three. Start with a story, not with "Today I'm going to talk about". Use pauses; silence is powerful. And end with a clear call to action, so people know exactly what you want them to do.

reading.text: On 28 August 1963, more than a quarter of a million people gathered in Washington, D.C., to demand equal rights for African Americans. The final speaker of the day was Martin Luther King Jr. His prepared text was powerful but formal, and for most of the speech he followed it closely. Then something unexpected happened. Near the end, the gospel singer Mahalia Jackson, who was standing nearby, called out to him: "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" King put his notes aside and began to speak from memory and from the heart. The words "I have a dream" were not in the written version of the speech at all. He had used the phrase in earlier speeches, but that afternoon, repeating it again and again, he turned it into one of the most famous passages in the history of public speaking. Such was its impact that, decades later, the speech is still studied in schools around the world. Its power came partly from its content, but also from its form. King used repetition, a technique known as anaphora, to build a rhythm that rose steadily towards a crescendo. He combined vivid images with references that his audience already knew and respected, from the American Declaration of Independence to the Bible. And he balanced pathos with logos, describing injustice in concrete detail before presenting his vision of the future. The story offers an important lesson for anyone who has to speak in public. Preparation matters, and King had spent years developing his ideas and his style. Yet the most memorable moment of his career came when he was willing to depart from his script and respond to the people in front of him. Great rhetoric, it seems, is not only about what we plan to say. It is also about listening to the audience, and having the courage to speak when the moment arrives.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today's topic is no laughing matter: we're talking about laughter itself. My guest is Dr Layla Farouk, a psychologist. Layla, why do we laugh?

Most people would say "because something is funny", but the research suggests otherwise. The American neuroscientist Robert Provine spent years listening to people laughing in shopping centres, streets and offices.
What did he find?
That most laughter has very little to do with jokes. Only about one in five laughs followed anything that resembled a joke. People laughed at ordinary comments like "See you later" or "I know!"
So what is laughter for?

Mainly for connecting with other people. Provine found that we're about thirty times more likely to laugh when we're with others than when we're alone. Laughter is a signal: "I'm friendly, we're on the same side."
Is it uniquely human?
Not at all. Chimpanzees and other apes make a panting sound when they play and tickle each other. It's very likely that our laughter evolved from that, long before we had language.
Is there any practical advice here?
If you want people to like you, don't worry about being funny. Just be someone people feel relaxed with. The laughter will follow.

reading.text: In 2001, the British psychologist Richard Wiseman launched an unusual scientific experiment. Its aim was to discover the world's funniest joke. People from all over the world were invited to submit their favourite jokes to a website and to rate those submitted by others. By the end of the project, the researchers had received more than forty thousand jokes and almost two million ratings from people in around seventy countries. The winning joke went roughly like this. Two hunters are walking through a forest when one of them suddenly collapses. His friend calls the emergency services in a panic and says, "I think my friend is dead! What should I do?" The operator replies calmly, "Don't worry. First, let's make sure he's dead." There is a silence, then the sound of a gunshot. The hunter comes back to the phone and asks, "OK, now what?" Why does this joke work, when so many others fail? Scholars have proposed three main theories of humour. The oldest, which goes back to ancient Greece, suggests that we laugh when we feel superior to someone else. A second theory, associated with Sigmund Freud, claims that laughter releases nervous energy. The third and most widely accepted theory focuses on incongruity: we laugh when two ideas that do not belong together suddenly meet. The hunter joke contains all three. We feel superior to the foolish hunter, the dark subject creates tension, and the punchline depends on an incongruity between two meanings of "make sure". Wiseman's experiment also showed how much humour varies. People in different countries tended to prefer different types of jokes, and what one group found hilarious, another found merely confusing. Perhaps the most important finding, however, was the simplest one: there is no single joke that everybody finds funny. Humour, like language itself, depends on who is listening.

dialogue.en: The Secret of Getting to Yes

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Whether you're buying a car or settling a war, you're negotiating. Professor Karim Aziz teaches negotiation at a business school. Karim, what's the biggest mistake people make?
They argue about positions instead of interests. Let me tell you a classic story. Two sisters are fighting over a single orange. In the end, they cut it in half.
That sounds fair.
It sounds fair, but it's a poor outcome. One sister wanted the juice; the other wanted the peel to bake a cake. If they had asked each other why, both could have had everything they wanted.
So the key question is "why"?

Exactly. This idea was made famous by a book called Getting to Yes, written in 1981 by Roger Fisher and William Ury at Harvard. Their advice was simple: separate the people from the problem, focus on interests, not positions, and invent options that benefit both sides.
What if the other side is much more powerful?

Then you need to know your best alternative if the talks fail. Fisher and Ury called it your BATNA: your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If your alternative is strong, you can walk away. If it's weak, you should work on improving it before you sit down at the table.
One last tip?
Listen more than you speak. The person who asks the best questions usually gets the best deal.

reading.en: The Table-Tennis Ball That Changed the World

reading.text: In the spring of 1971, the United States and the People's Republic of China had not had official relations for more than twenty years. Travel between the two countries was almost impossible, and each government regarded the other with deep suspicion. Few people would have predicted that the first crack in this wall would be made by a young table-tennis player. At the world championships in Japan that April, an American player named Glenn Cowan missed his team bus and, by chance, climbed onto the bus carrying the Chinese team. The Chinese players had been instructed not to communicate with Americans, and for a moment nobody spoke. Then the Chinese star Zhuang Zedong walked over, shook Cowan's hand and gave him a silk picture of a famous Chinese mountain as a gift. Photographers captured the moment, and the images appeared in newspapers around the world. Within days, to the surprise of almost everyone, China invited the American team to visit. The players toured Chinese cities, played friendly matches and were received by the Chinese premier, Zhou Enlai. Behind the scenes, diplomats on both sides recognised an opportunity. Secret talks followed, and in February 1972 President Richard Nixon became the first American president to visit China. Historians still debate how much the table-tennis players really changed. The governments had already been looking for ways to improve relations for strategic reasons, and they might well have done so eventually without any help from sport. What "ping-pong diplomacy" provided was a safe, human first step: a way to test public reaction without either side losing face. The story remains a powerful example of soft power. Formal negotiations are essential, but sometimes the most important message is carried not by ministers or envoys, but by a small gesture of goodwill that reminds both sides they are dealing with people rather than enemies.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Over half the world's population is thought to speak more than one language. What does that do to the brain? Dr Rami Yousif is a cognitive scientist.
It's a fascinating question. Every time a bilingual person speaks, both languages are active in the brain at the same time. So they constantly have to choose one and quietly ignore the other.
That sounds exhausting.

It's more like exercise. The Canadian psychologist Ellen Bialystok suggested that this daily practice strengthens executive function, the skills we use to focus, switch between tasks and ignore distractions.
Is that proven?

Honestly, it's controversial. Some early studies found clear advantages. One study even suggested that bilingual patients developed symptoms of dementia about four years later than monolingual patients. But other researchers have tried to repeat these experiments and found much smaller effects, or none at all.
So what can we say for sure?

We can say for sure that bilingualism does no harm. For decades, parents were told that two languages would confuse their children. That's simply not true. Children can learn two or even three languages from birth without any problem.
Any advice for families abroad?
Keep your heritage language alive at home. The children will learn the local language at school anyway, but if you don't speak your own language to them, they may lose it completely.

reading.en: Does Your Language Shape How You Think?
reading.text: If you ask a speaker of English to describe where an object is, they will probably say it is on their left or right. Ask a speaker of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, and the answer will be very different. Their language has no words for left and right. Instead, speakers describe everything using the directions of the compass: there is an ant on your north leg, or move the cup a little to the east. As a result, they keep track of north, south, east and west at every moment, even indoors and in unfamiliar places. Researchers have found that they can point in the right direction with an accuracy that astonishes visitors. Examples like this lie at the heart of an old and controversial idea known as linguistic relativity: the theory that the language we speak influences the way we think. In its strongest form, the theory claims that language determines thought, so that we cannot think about things for which we have no words. Very few scholars today accept this extreme version. After all, if it were true, translation would be impossible, and new words could never be invented. A weaker version, however, has gained considerable support. Russian, for example, has two separate basic words for light blue and dark blue. In one well-known experiment, Russian speakers were slightly faster than English speakers at telling the difference between two shades of blue when the shades fell on either side of that boundary. Language did not stop English speakers from seeing the difference; it simply made Russian speakers a little quicker to notice it. For learners of a new language, the implications are encouraging. Learning another language does not simply give you new words for the same ideas. To some extent, it gives you new habits of attention: new ways of noticing time, space, relationships and politeness that your first language may have taught you to overlook.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Every day we see hundreds of headlines. How can we tell which ones to trust? I'm joined by Zainab Hamid, a professional fact-checker.
Thanks. The first thing I'd say is: don't trust your feelings. If a story makes you very angry or very excited, that's a warning sign, not a reason to share it.
So what should we do?

A digital literacy expert called Mike Caulfield created a simple method called SIFT. S is for Stop. I is for Investigate the source. F is for Find better coverage, and T is for Trace claims back to their original context.
What's the most useful step?

Probably the second. In 2017, researchers at Stanford University compared professional fact-checkers with history professors and university students. The fact-checkers were much faster and more accurate.
Why? Were they smarter?

No. They simply read differently. The students and professors read the website carefully from top to bottom. The fact-checkers left the website almost immediately and opened new tabs to see what other sources said about it. Researchers call this lateral reading.
So, read sideways, not down.
Exactly. A website can look very professional and still be completely unreliable. What other people say about a source is often more revealing than what the source says about itself.

reading.text: On the evening of 30 October 1938, a young actor named Orson Welles broadcast a radio drama based on H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds. The programme was presented as a series of urgent news bulletins describing an invasion from Mars. The next morning, newspapers across the United States carried dramatic headlines. Thousands of listeners, they reported, had fled their homes in terror, jammed the roads and flooded police stations with calls. The story of the great Martian panic has been retold ever since, and it is still cited as proof of the extraordinary power of the media to deceive the public. There is just one problem: it was very likely exaggerated. Later researchers who examined the evidence found surprisingly little to support the newspapers' claims. Relatively few Americans were even listening; the programme was up against one of the most popular shows of the day on another station. One national survey conducted that night reportedly found that only around two per cent of people questioned were tuned in to the broadcast. Many of those who did hear it presumably understood that it was fiction, since the programme was introduced as a drama. Why, then, did the newspapers tell such a different story? One explanation is that they had a motive. Radio had been taking advertising money away from newspapers for years, and a story showing that radio was irresponsible and dangerous was, arguably, too tempting to resist. Most of the reports were based on a handful of anecdotes rather than systematic evidence, and they were repeated so often that they came to be accepted as fact. The irony is hard to miss. The famous example of the media spreading panic about fake news was, to a large extent, itself a piece of misleading news. It is a reminder that the most dangerous falsehoods are not always the ones we suspect, but the ones we have heard so many times that we never think to check.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Before we begin, here's a quick puzzle. A bat and a ball cost one dollar ten in total. The bat costs one dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? Dr Huda Salman, what do most people say?
Most people say ten cents, immediately. And they're wrong. If the ball cost ten cents, the bat would cost one dollar ten, and the total would be one dollar twenty. The correct answer is five cents.
Why do so many of us get it wrong?

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, explained it with two systems of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive. System 2 is slow, careful and effortful.
And the ten-cent answer comes from System 1?

Exactly. System 1 jumps to an answer that feels right, and System 2 is lazy; it often accepts that answer without checking. Kahneman described this in his famous book Thinking, Fast and Slow, published in 2011.
Is System 1 the enemy, then?
Not at all. Without it, we couldn't drive a car, read a face or avoid danger. The problem is that it uses mental shortcuts, and those shortcuts lead to predictable biases.
How can we protect ourselves?

For important decisions, slow down deliberately. Ask yourself: what would make this answer wrong? And be careful when you feel very sure. Strong confidence often comes from System 1, not from evidence.

reading.text: In 2000, two psychologists, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper, published a study that would become one of the most quoted experiments in modern psychology. On different days in a California supermarket, they set up a table offering free samples of jam. Sometimes the table displayed twenty-four varieties; at other times, only six. The larger display attracted more attention: around sixty per cent of passing shoppers stopped to look, compared with forty per cent at the smaller one. But when it came to buying, the result was reversed. About thirty per cent of those who had seen six jams went on to buy a jar, while only three per cent of those who had seen twenty-four did so. The researchers concluded that too much choice can be demotivating. The study fitted neatly with a popular book by the psychologist Barry Schwartz, The Paradox of Choice, which argued that modern life overwhelms us with options. Schwartz drew on an idea proposed decades earlier by the economist Herbert Simon, who distinguished between people who search for the best possible option and those who accept the first option that is good enough. Schwartz suggested that the first group, whom he called maximisers, often end up less satisfied than the second, even when they make objectively better choices. Yet the story has an important twist. When other researchers tried to repeat the jam experiment and similar studies, the results were mixed. A review of dozens of experiments found that, on average, the effect of having more options was close to zero. Choice overload seems to occur only under certain conditions: when options are hard to compare, when people do not know what they want, or when they are under time pressure. The lesson is a subtle one. Having choices is not, in itself, harmful. What overwhelms us is being asked to choose without clear information or enough time. A shop with fewer but better-explained options may therefore serve its customers better than one that simply offers more.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. These days, arguments online seem to generate more heat than light. Dr Faisal Ali coaches university debate teams. Faisal, is there a better way to disagree?
I think so. My favourite advice comes from the philosopher Daniel Dennett. He suggested a set of rules for criticising someone's views, which he named after the psychologist Anatol Rapoport.
What are the rules?

First, restate your opponent's position so clearly and fairly that they say, "Thanks, I wish I'd put it that way." Second, list any points where you agree. Third, mention anything you've learned from them. Only then are you allowed to say a word of criticism.
That sounds very slow.

It is slower, but it's far more effective. If you attack a weaker version of someone's argument, a straw man, they'll simply feel misunderstood and dig in. If you show that you really understand them, they're much more likely to listen.
Debaters call that "steelmanning", don't they?
Yes. Instead of a straw man, you build a steel man: the strongest possible version of the other side's case. If your argument can defeat that, it's a good argument.
And what about winning?
In a competition, winning matters. In real life, the goal isn't to win; it's to get closer to the truth. Under no circumstances should you mistake a loud argument for a good one.

reading.text: If people are shown clear evidence that one of their beliefs is wrong, surely they will change their minds? For a long time, many researchers feared the opposite. In 2010, two political scientists, Brendan Nyhan and Jason Reifler, published experiments suggesting that correcting false beliefs could sometimes backfire. In some cases, people who were shown corrections ended up believing the original false claim even more strongly. The idea of a "backfire effect" spread rapidly. Journalists wrote that facts were useless against strongly held beliefs, and some people concluded that there was little point in correcting misinformation at all. Little did they suspect that the story was about to change. Over the following years, other researchers, including Nyhan himself, tried to repeat these findings on a much larger scale. In study after study involving thousands of participants and dozens of different claims, they found that the backfire effect was extremely rare. In most cases, people who saw a correction moved at least slightly towards the truth, even when the correction contradicted their political views. Only when the subject was closely connected to a person's sense of identity did resistance become strong, and even then corrections rarely made things worse. This does not mean that changing minds is easy. People tend to interpret evidence in ways that protect what they already believe, a process psychologists call motivated reasoning. A single correction is unlikely to overturn a deep-seated belief, and the way a correction is delivered matters a great deal. Corrections from trusted sources, presented respectfully and without mocking the other person, are far more effective than angry lectures. The history of the backfire effect contains a lesson of its own. A dramatic finding, repeated often enough, became widely accepted before it had been properly tested. Not until other scientists put it to the test did a more nuanced picture emerge. That, in the end, is exactly how critical thinking is supposed to work.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. If you've driven past an oil field in southern Iraq at night, you've seen giant flames burning in the sky. Dr Ahmed Jassim is an energy engineer. Ahmed, what are those flames?
That's gas flaring. When oil comes out of the ground, natural gas comes with it. If there's no system to capture and use that gas, the easiest option is to burn it.
Is that a big problem?

It's huge. According to World Bank data, Iraq is among the three countries that flare the most gas in the world. We're literally burning a valuable resource, and at the same time we import gas and electricity from abroad.
That sounds absurd.

It is. And it's not just an economic problem. Flaring releases carbon dioxide, and incomplete burning releases methane and fine particulates. People living near the oil fields have long complained about health problems.
Why hasn't it stopped?

Capturing the gas requires pipelines, processing plants and a lot of investment. Projects have been announced many times, but progress has been slow. The good news is that several capture projects are now under way.
And what about solar energy?

Iraq has excellent sunshine for most of the year, so solar power has enormous potential. Combining captured gas with solar could cut power cuts, reduce pollution and save billions of dollars. The resources are already here; what we need is the will to use them wisely.

reading.text: It seems logical that making machines more efficient should reduce the amount of energy we use. If a new car travels twice as far on the same amount of fuel, surely it will burn half as much? In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons observed something that challenged this assumption. Britain's steam engines had become far more efficient at using coal, yet the country's total coal consumption had not fallen. On the contrary, it had risen dramatically. Jevons argued that the improvements were the cause rather than the cure. Because steam power had become cheaper, it was used in many more factories, mines and railways, thereby increasing the overall demand for coal. This counter-intuitive idea became known as the Jevons paradox, and economists today speak more generally of the "rebound effect". When something becomes more efficient, it often becomes cheaper to use, and people respond by using more of it. Owners of fuel-efficient cars may drive longer distances. Cheaper lighting encourages us to light more rooms for longer. Lower costs in one area may also leave people with more money to spend on other energy-hungry products, such as flights. How large is the rebound effect in practice? Here the evidence is mixed. In most cases, studies suggest, efficiency still produces real savings, but the savings are smaller than engineers predict, because part of the benefit is eaten up by increased use. In a few cases, the rebound can be large enough to cancel out the savings entirely. None of this means that efficiency is a bad idea. Rather, it suggests that efficiency alone is unlikely to solve problems that stem from overconsumption. To achieve lasting reductions, economists argue, improvements in technology need to be combined with policies such as carbon taxes or limits on emissions, which make sure that the energy saved is not simply used somewhere else.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Migration is one of the most emotional topics in politics, but what do the numbers actually say? Dr Sara Mahdi is a migration researcher.

Let's start with a surprising fact. According to the United Nations, there were around 281 million international migrants in 2020. That sounds enormous, but it's only about three point six per cent of the world's population. The vast majority of people live in the country where they were born.
So why do some people leave?

Researchers often talk about push and pull factors. Push factors drive people away: war, persecution, poverty or environmental disasters. Pull factors attract them: jobs, safety, education or family who are already there.
Is that a new idea?

Not at all. As early as 1885, a geographer called Ernst Ravenstein published what he called "the laws of migration". One of his findings still holds true: most migrants move only a short distance, often within their own country.
What about the idea that everyone wants to go to Europe?

The evidence doesn't support it. Most refugees stay in neighbouring countries, hoping to return home. Interestingly, the very poorest people are often the least likely to migrate far, simply because long journeys are expensive.
Any final thought?
Behind every statistic is a person making one of the hardest decisions of their life. The more we understand the reasons, the better our policies are likely to be.

reading.en: From Brain Drain to Brain Circulation
reading.text: For decades, the departure of doctors, engineers and scientists from poorer countries was described with a single, gloomy phrase: the brain drain. Governments that had invested heavily in educating their young people watched them leave for better salaries abroad, and the loss seemed permanent. The more talented the graduate, it was assumed, the less likely they were ever to return. Since the 1990s, however, researchers have painted a considerably more complex picture. The economist and geographer AnnaLee Saxenian studied engineers from Taiwan, India and China who had worked in California's Silicon Valley. She found that many of them did not simply leave home for good. Some returned to set up their own companies, bringing with them technical knowledge, management experience and, crucially, networks of contacts. Others stayed abroad but invested in businesses at home or helped local firms win international contracts. Saxenian called them "the new Argonauts", after the adventurers of Greek mythology, and described the process as brain circulation rather than brain drain. Taiwan offers a striking example. From the 1980s onwards, a new science park near the city of Hsinchu attracted returning engineers, and the island went on to become one of the most important centres of the global electronics industry. Government policy undoubtedly played a major role, but the returning engineers were arguably every bit as important to the island's success. None of this means that the brain drain is a myth. Small countries can lose a large share of their doctors and nurses, with serious consequences for public health. The difference between drain and circulation seems to depend largely on conditions at home. Where there is stability, opportunity and a welcoming attitude towards those who return, emigrants are far more likely to come back, or at least to stay connected. Where these conditions are absent, the drain is likely to continue.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. It killed an estimated three hundred million people in the twentieth century alone, and then it disappeared. We're talking about smallpox. Dr Nour Abbas is a public health historian.
Smallpox is the only human disease that we've ever completely eradicated. The World Health Organization declared it gone in 1980.
How was that possible?

Several things came together. There was an effective vaccine. Smallpox only infected humans, so there was no animal reservoir where it could hide. And the disease had very visible symptoms, so cases were easy to identify.
Did they vaccinate everyone in the world?

No, and that's the clever part. Instead of trying to vaccinate whole populations, health workers used a strategy called ring vaccination. Whenever a case was found, they vaccinated everyone around the patient: family, neighbours, contacts. That created a ring of immunity the virus couldn't break through.
When was the last natural case?
In 1977, in Somalia. A hospital cook called Ali Maow Maalin. He survived, and he later spent years working to eradicate polio.
And is polio close to being eradicated?

Very close. Wild polio now survives in only a handful of places, mainly Pakistan and Afghanistan. But the last steps are always the hardest. Conflict, vaccine hesitancy and difficult terrain all make that final push extremely challenging.

reading.text: In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find that mould had contaminated one of his laboratory dishes. Around the mould, the bacteria he had been growing had died. His accidental discovery led to penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, and transformed medicine. Infections that had once been a death sentence could now be cured in days. Yet Fleming himself was among the first to warn of a danger. In his Nobel Prize lecture in 1945, he cautioned that bacteria could become resistant if the drug was used carelessly. Eight decades later, his warning has proved alarmingly accurate. Every time antibiotics are used, a small number of bacteria may survive because of random mutations. These survivors multiply, and over time, resistant strains become more common. The problem is made worse when antibiotics are overused or misused: prescribed for viral infections such as colds, on which they have no effect; stopped too early; or given routinely to healthy farm animals to make them grow faster. A major study published in 2022 estimated that, in 2019, bacterial antimicrobial resistance was directly responsible for around 1.27 million deaths worldwide, more than either HIV or malaria. The vast majority of these deaths occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where access to newer medicines is limited and sanitation is often poor. A widely cited British review warned that, without action, the annual death toll could reach as many as ten million by 2050. Solving the problem will require action on several fronts. Doctors need faster tests to tell whether an infection is bacterial. Farmers need to reduce their use of antibiotics. And because developing new antibiotics is expensive and unprofitable, governments may need to reward companies for creating drugs that, ideally, will be used as rarely as possible. Fleming's accidental gift, in other words, can only be protected by very deliberate care.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. What do a tiny sleeping bag and a billion-dollar company have in common? Design thinking. Rana Saeed is a product designer. Rana, what is design thinking?
It's an approach to solving problems that starts with people rather than with technology. Designers usually describe five stages: empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test.
Can you give an example?

My favourite is a project from Stanford University's design school. In 2007, a group of students were asked to design a cheaper incubator for premature babies in developing countries. A typical incubator cost around twenty thousand dollars.
So they designed a cheaper incubator?

That's the interesting part. When they visited Nepal, they discovered that the real pain point wasn't the price. Most premature babies were born in villages, far from hospitals, where there was often no reliable electricity. An expensive machine in a city hospital couldn't help them.
So what did they make?

Something like a small sleeping bag with a pouch of special wax. You heat the wax, and it keeps the baby at the right temperature for hours, with no electricity needed. It cost a small fraction of the price of a traditional incubator, and it has since been used for many thousands of babies.
That's ingenious.
It is, and it shows why empathy comes first. With the wrong question, even brilliant engineers will build the wrong product.

reading.text: In the 1990s, Japan's high-speed bullet trains had an unexpected problem. Whenever a train entered a tunnel at high speed, it pushed a wall of air ahead of it. When the train came out the other end, the air was released with a loud boom that disturbed people living nearby. With strict noise limits in place, the railway company could not simply make the trains faster. The solution came from an engineer named Eiji Nakatsu, who happened to be a keen birdwatcher. He knew that kingfishers dive from the air into water to catch fish, and that they enter the water with hardly a splash. The secret, he realised, lay in the shape of the bird's long, pointed beak. Nakatsu's team redesigned the front of the train to resemble a kingfisher's beak. The new trains were quieter, and, according to the company, they also used less electricity and travelled faster than before. Nakatsu's train is a famous example of biomimicry: the practice of solving human problems by studying how nature has already solved them. The idea is far from new. In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral returned from a walk with his dog and noticed that small seed pods had stuck firmly to his clothes and to the dog's fur. Looking at them under a microscope, he saw that they were covered in tiny hooks. The result, after years of experimentation, was Velcro. In the 1990s, the architect Mick Pearce designed an office building in Harare, Zimbabwe, that keeps cool without conventional air conditioning. He was inspired by termite mounds, which maintain a stable internal temperature through a clever system of air channels. Supporters of biomimicry argue that nature has had millions of years to test its designs. All things considered, it would be strange not to learn from the most experienced engineer on the planet.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. How much of your life is decided before you're even born? Dr Hassan Kareem is an economist who studies inequality.

Probably more than most of us would like to admit. The economist Branko Milanovic has calculated that the country you're born in explains more than half of the differences in income between people around the world.
More than education or hard work?

In global terms, yes. A cleaner in a rich country can earn more than a doctor in a poor one. Milanovic calls this a kind of "citizenship premium". It's not about how hard you work; it's about where you happen to be born.
And within a country?

That's where social mobility comes in. The American economist Raj Chetty and his colleagues used tax records for millions of people. They found that around ninety per cent of Americans born in 1940 went on to earn more than their parents. For those born in 1980, it was only about half.
Why such a big fall?

Mainly because growth slowed and, crucially, because the benefits of growth went increasingly to people at the top. What really matters for mobility isn't just how fast the economy grows; it's how widely the gains are shared.
Is there any good news?

Yes. Chetty's research also shows that the neighbourhood where a child grows up makes a real difference. Children who move to better areas at a young age earn significantly more as adults. In other words, opportunity can be changed by policy. It isn't fixed by birth.

reading.text: Who becomes an inventor? It is tempting to assume that the answer is simple: the most talented people. A group of economists led by Raj Chetty set out to test this assumption by linking patent records with tax data for more than a million Americans. What they found was striking. Children born into the richest one per cent of families were around ten times as likely to become inventors as children from families with below-average incomes. At first, this might seem to reflect differences in ability. To check, the researchers examined maths test scores from primary school. Talent clearly mattered: children with high scores were more likely to become inventors. But it explained only a small part of the gap. Among children who scored in the top five per cent, those from rich families were still far more likely to go on to invent than equally gifted children from poorer backgrounds. It wasn't until the researchers looked at where children grew up that a clearer picture emerged. Children who grew up in areas with many inventors were much more likely to become inventors themselves, often in the same field. Girls who grew up surrounded by female inventors were more likely to invent than girls who did not. What seemed to matter most was exposure: simply knowing people who did this kind of work, and seeing it as a possible future. The researchers concluded that the United States was losing a vast number of potential inventors, children who had the ability but never had the chance. They called them "lost Einsteins". The implications reach far beyond America. In any country where talent is equally distributed but opportunity is not, the cost of inequality is not only paid by the poor. It is paid by everyone, in the form of cures that are never found and inventions that are never made.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today's story begins in Iraq more than four thousand years ago. Dr Ali Mansour is an Assyriologist. Ali, what is the Epic of Gilgamesh?

It's the story of Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk who is two-thirds god and one-third human. He's arrogant at the start, but after his best friend Enkidu dies, he sets out on a journey to find the secret of eternal life.
Does he find it?

Almost. He finds a plant that can make him young again, but while he's bathing, a snake steals it. He returns to Uruk with nothing except wisdom: he learns that humans can't live for ever, but they can leave something lasting behind, like the great walls of his city.
How was the story rediscovered?

In the 1850s, archaeologists excavating the ancient city of Nineveh, near Mosul, found the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. Thousands of clay tablets were sent to the British Museum. In 1872, a young scholar named George Smith was reading one of them when he realised it described a great flood and a man who built a boat.
A story very similar to Noah's?
Exactly. According to one account, Smith was so excited that he jumped up and began to undress in front of his colleagues! His discovery caused a sensation.
And there's a modern chapter too, isn't there?

Yes. A small tablet with part of the epic, known as the Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, was looted from Iraq and ended up in the United States. In 2021, it was finally returned to Iraq. After thousands of years, part of the story has come home.

reading.text: Every time you check the time, you are using an idea that was born in ancient Iraq. Why are there sixty seconds in a minute and sixty minutes in an hour, rather than a hundred? The answer lies with the Sumerians and later the Babylonians, who used a sexagesimal number system based on sixty. Sixty is a remarkably practical number: it can be divided evenly by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty and thirty. The same system gave us the 360 degrees of a circle, and it is still used every day by pilots, sailors and astronomers. Time is only the beginning. Writing itself appears to have emerged in the city of Uruk around 3200 BC. Interestingly, the first writers were not poets or priests but accountants. The earliest tablets record quantities of grain, beer and livestock, and the signs were pressed into wet clay with a cut reed. Over the following centuries, this practical system of record-keeping was to develop into cuneiform, a script that could express laws, letters, prayers and epic poetry, and that was used for around three thousand years. Mesopotamia also gave the world some of its earliest written laws. Around 2100 BC, King Ur-Nammu of Ur codified a set of laws that predates the famous code of Hammurabi by several centuries. Remarkably, many of its punishments were fines rather than physical penalties. Alongside these achievements came the first cities, monumental temples, schools for scribes and detailed observations of the stars. None of this would have been possible without the two great rivers. The Tigris and the Euphrates carried silt that made the land fertile, but their floods were unpredictable. To survive, communities had to cooperate, build irrigation canals and keep records. In this sense, the challenges of the land may have been the very thing that pushed its people to invent civilisation.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. What makes a good life? Money? Fame? Success? Dr Maryam Hadi is a psychologist who has followed one of the most remarkable studies ever conducted.

It's called the Harvard Study of Adult Development. It began in 1938 and followed 724 young men for the rest of their lives: some were students at Harvard, and others grew up in poor neighbourhoods of Boston. Later, the researchers added their wives and children.
Eighty years of data! What did they find?

The clearest message was by no means what the young men expected. When they were young, most of them believed fame and wealth would make them happy. But the people who were happiest and healthiest in old age were those who had the warmest relationships.
Not the richest?
Not at all. In fact, how satisfied people were with their relationships at the age of fifty was a better predictor of their health at eighty than their cholesterol levels.
That's extraordinary. What about loneliness?
Loneliness turned out to be genuinely harmful. Lonely people were less happy, their health declined earlier, and their memory tended to get worse sooner.
Does it have to be lots of friends?

No. Quality matters far more than quantity. One or two people you can truly rely on are worth more than a hundred acquaintances. The study's current director, Robert Waldinger, puts it simply: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.

reading.en: Is Stress Really Bad for You?
reading.text: Few pieces of health advice are repeated as often as this one: stress is bad for you. Stress has been linked to heart disease, poor sleep and weakened immunity, and millions of people now try to remove it from their lives altogether. Yet a growing body of research suggests that the picture is by no means that simple. In one widely discussed study published in 2012, researchers in the United States analysed data on around 29,000 adults. Participants had been asked two questions: how much stress they had experienced in the previous year, and whether they believed that stress was harmful to their health. The researchers then examined death records over the following eight years. As expected, people who had experienced a lot of stress were more likely to die early, but only if they also believed that stress was harmful. Among people with high levels of stress who did not see it as harmful, the risk was no higher than among those with very little stress. Other experiments point in the same direction. The psychologist Alia Crum and her colleagues found that people who were shown short videos presenting stress as something that can sharpen focus and help us grow reported fewer negative symptoms and performed better under pressure than those shown videos about its dangers. None of this means that stress is good for you in all circumstances. Chronic stress caused by poverty, violence or illness does real damage, and it cannot be solved simply by changing one's attitude. What these studies do suggest is that the meaning we give to everyday pressures matters. A racing heart before an exam is not necessarily a sign that something is wrong; it may be the very energy our body is giving us to meet the challenge. Seen this way, the aim is not a life without stress, but a healthier relationship with it.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. How long do you spend looking at a painting in a museum? Dr Lina Wahbi is an art historian. Lina, any guesses?

Most people think they spend a few minutes. In 2001, two researchers secretly timed visitors at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The average time spent in front of a famous painting was about twenty-seven seconds.
Twenty-seven seconds? That includes reading the label?
It does! Many visitors spend more time reading the label than looking at the work itself. And today, a lot of people spend those seconds taking a photo.
Is that a problem?
It means we miss a great deal. A professor at Harvard, Jennifer Roberts, asks her students to look at a single painting for three hours.
Three hours! Isn't that torture?

That's what the students think at first. But she says they discover details they would never have noticed: a reflection, a strange shadow, a figure hidden in the background. The painting reveals itself slowly, and the students learn that patience is a skill.
What can our listeners try?

Next time you visit a museum, choose just one work. Look at it for ten minutes without your phone. Notice the colours first, then the composition, then the details. Ask yourself what the artist wants you to feel. I promise it will be a far cry from walking past fifty paintings in an hour.

reading.text: Anyone who has crossed Tahrir Square in central Baghdad has seen it: a long white wall raised high above the ground, carrying a series of bronze figures. This is the Monument of Freedom, or Nasb al-Hurriya, the masterpiece of the Iraqi artist Jewad Selim. To understand it, however, the viewer needs to know something that many passers-by do not: the monument is meant to be read from right to left, like a line of Arabic poetry. Selim designed the work after the revolution of 1958, and it tells the story of modern Iraq in a sequence of scenes. On the right, a horse rears up, suggesting the chaos of the past. Further along, figures represent suffering, imprisonment and protest. At the centre, a soldier breaks through the bars of a prison, while a figure holding a torch symbolises the moment of liberation. The scenes on the left are calmer: a mother with her child, farmers, and a worker, suggesting a future built on peace, agriculture and industry. Selim drew on several sources. Elements of the composition recall ancient Assyrian and Babylonian reliefs, which also tell stories through rows of figures. At the same time, the bodies are simplified in a distinctly modern way. This combination was no accident. Selim, together with the painter Shakir Hassan Al Said, had founded the Baghdad Group for Modern Art in 1951, and the former believed that Iraqi artists should create a modern style rooted in their own heritage rather than copying Europe. Sadly, Selim died in 1961, before the monument was completed. The work was finished under the supervision of his assistant, the sculptor Mohammed Ghani Hikmat. Decades later, it remains one of the most recognisable images of Baghdad. Like all great works of art, it is open to interpretation, but its central message speaks for itself: a nation's story, written in bronze, from darkness towards light.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Today, a famous puzzle. Suppose a runaway train is heading towards five workers on the track. You're standing next to a lever. If you pull it, the train moves to another track, where it will kill one worker instead. Would you pull it? Professor Sami Nasser is a philosopher.
Most people say yes. Saving five lives at the cost of one seems the lesser evil. That's a utilitarian answer: choose the action that produces the best overall outcome.
But there's a second version, isn't there?
Yes. This time, you're standing on a bridge above the track, next to a very large man. The only way to stop the train is to push him off the bridge. Again, one dies and five are saved.
That feels completely different.

Exactly, and that's the puzzle. The numbers are the same, yet most people refuse to push. The philosopher Philippa Foot introduced this kind of problem in 1967, and it's still debated today. It suggests that our moral intuitions don't just count outcomes; we also care about how we cause them.
Is this just an academic game?

Not any more. Self-driving cars may one day face similar choices. Researchers at MIT created an online game called the Moral Machine and collected around forty million decisions from people in over two hundred countries and territories. They found some universal preferences, like saving more lives, but also clear cultural differences.
So what's the right answer?
Philosophers have been arguing about that for decades. But perhaps the real value of the problem is that it forces us to explain why we believe what we believe.

reading.text: Imagine a machine that could give you any experience you wanted. Scientists would connect your brain to it, and from that moment you would believe, completely and convincingly, that you were writing a great novel, winning a gold medal or falling in love. You would never know that you were actually lying in a tank in a laboratory. Suppose you could plug in for the rest of your life. Would you do it? The American philosopher Robert Nozick proposed this thought experiment in 1974. His aim was to challenge a popular philosophical idea known as hedonism: the view that pleasure is the only thing that has intrinsic value. If hedonism were true, Nozick argued, we should all be eager to plug in, since the machine would give us far more pleasure than real life ever could. Yet most people, when they think about it, refuse. Nozick suggested several reasons. We want to actually do things, not just have the experience of doing them. We want to be a certain kind of person, rather than a body floating in a tank. And we want contact with reality, not with an illusion, however pleasant. If this is right, then pleasure cannot be the only thing that matters. For decades, the experiment seemed to offer a clear lesson. More recently, however, some philosophers have questioned it. In one study, people were asked to imagine that they had already been living in such a machine without knowing it, and were now given the chance to leave and return to a real life that was much less pleasant. Many chose to stay. This suggests that our reaction to the original experiment may partly reflect a simple preference for whatever is familiar, rather than a deep love of reality. The question, then, remains open. But perhaps that is what makes a good thought experiment so valuable: it does not end an argument; it begins one.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Most of the apps on your phone are free. So how do they make money? Huda Karim is a privacy researcher.
Mainly by collecting data about you and using it to sell targeted advertising. There's a well-known saying in the tech world: if you're not paying for the product, you are the product.
What kind of data are we talking about?

Far more than most people imagine. Your location, the websites you visit, how long you look at a post, what you buy, even how fast you type. On its own, each piece seems harmless. Aggregated, it can reveal your health, your income, your relationships and your political views.
Can you give an example?

A famous one comes from a newspaper report in 2012 about an American shop. According to the report, its analysts found that changes in what women bought, such as unscented lotion and certain vitamins, could predict a pregnancy. The shop then sent baby-product coupons to a teenage girl, and, the story goes, her father found out before she told him.
That's quite disturbing.

It is. And the shop didn't need to break any law. That's why many experts argue that the issue isn't only security; it's power. Companies know a great deal about us, while we know very little about them.
What can ordinary users do?

Start small. Check which apps can see your location and turn it off where it isn't needed. Opt out of personalised advertising. And before you click "accept", ask yourself one question: what am I giving away in return?

reading.text: In 1998, a Spanish newspaper published a short notice announcing the forced sale of a property belonging to a man named Mario Costeja González, who at the time was struggling to pay his debts. The debts were eventually paid, and life moved on. Yet more than a decade later, anyone who searched for his name online would still find the old notice among the first results. Costeja González argued that this information was no longer relevant and was damaging his reputation. He asked for it to be removed. The case went all the way to the Court of Justice of the European Union, which, in 2014, delivered a landmark ruling. In certain circumstances, the court decided, individuals have the right to ask search engines to remove links to information about them that is inaccurate, irrelevant or out of date. This became known as the right to be forgotten. Four years later, the principle was written into a much broader law. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in May 2018, gave people new rights with regard to their personal data, including the right to see what information companies hold about them and, in many cases, to have it deleted. Companies that fail to comply can be fined up to twenty million euros or four per cent of their worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Because the law applies to any company that handles the data of people in the EU, its influence has spread far beyond Europe, and many other countries have since introduced similar rules. Critics have raised concerns. Some argue that the right to be forgotten could be used by powerful people to hide information the public has a legitimate interest in knowing. Supporters reply that the right is not absolute and that requests must be balanced against freedom of expression. In light of how much of our lives is now recorded, the debate is only likely to grow.
