lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. Dr Yasmin Talib is a marine biologist. Yasmin, why do reefs matter so much?

Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they're home to around a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and provide food and income for hundreds of millions of people.
We often hear about coral bleaching. What actually happens?

Corals live in symbiosis with tiny algae that live inside their tissues. The algae give the coral food and its beautiful colours. When the water gets too warm, the coral becomes stressed and pushes the algae out. Without them, it turns white, which is what we call bleaching.
Does that mean the coral is dead?
Not immediately. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can come back and the coral can recover. But if the heat lasts too long, or happens too often, the coral starves and dies.
How often is it happening?

Far more often than before. Australia's Great Barrier Reef has suffered several mass bleaching events since 2016, when in the past they were rare. Reefs need years to recover, and they're simply not getting that time.
Is there any hope?

Yes. Scientists are growing heat-resistant corals and replanting damaged reefs. Marine reserves help reefs stay healthier. But in the end, the most important step is to cut emissions, because no amount of replanting can keep up with oceans that keep getting warmer.

reading.text: For thousands of years, the marshes of southern Iraq, where the Tigris and Euphrates spread out before reaching the sea, were among the largest wetlands in western Asia. Covering an area that once reached around fifteen thousand square kilometres, they supported a unique way of life. The Marsh Arabs lived on floating islands of reeds, built magnificent reed guest houses known as mudhif, travelled by narrow boats and raised water buffalo. The marshes were also an irreplaceable stop for migratory birds travelling between Siberia and Africa, and a breeding ground for fish that stocked the waters of the Gulf. During the 1990s, the marshes were deliberately drained through a vast network of canals and embankments. The results were catastrophic. By the early 2000s, satellite images showed that around ninety per cent of the original wetlands had disappeared, turning much of the area into salty desert. Most of the people who had lived there for generations were forced to leave, and several species, including a small bird called the Basra reed warbler, were pushed towards extinction. After 2003, local people began breaking down the embankments, and water flowed back into parts of the marshes. The speed of the recovery surprised many scientists. Reeds regenerated within months, fish returned, and birds that had not been seen for years were recorded again. In 2016, the marshes, together with several ancient Mesopotamian cities, were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Yet the story is far from over. Upstream dams in neighbouring countries, combined with drought and rising temperatures, have reduced the flow of water, and in dry years large areas of the marshes shrink once again. The marshes have shown that nature can regenerate remarkably quickly when given the chance. Whether they will be given that chance depends on decisions about water that are made far beyond their borders.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. In 2015, a group of researchers did something unusual: they tried to repeat a hundred published psychology studies. Dr Tariq Saleem is a research methods expert. Tariq, what happened?

The project was led by the psychologist Brian Nosek. Around 270 researchers repeated a hundred studies from respected journals as closely as possible. Only about a third of the replications produced the same statistically significant results as the originals.
A third? That's shocking.
It was a wake-up call. Similar problems have since been found in medicine, economics and other fields. People started talking about a replication crisis.
Does that mean the original scientists were cheating?

In most cases, no. The problems were more subtle. Many studies used small sample sizes, which makes chance results more likely. Researchers sometimes tried several analyses and reported only the ones that worked. And journals preferred exciting new findings to boring replications, so failed results were rarely published.
So should we stop trusting science?

Quite the opposite. The replication crisis was discovered by scientists themselves. That's how science is supposed to work: it corrects its own mistakes. Today, many researchers publish their plans before they collect data, share their data openly and run larger studies.
Any advice for students reading research?
Ask three questions. How big was the sample? Has the result been replicated? And who funded the study? A single exciting study is a starting point, not a final answer.

reading.text: In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital had two maternity clinics, and a terrible puzzle. In the first, where women were cared for by doctors and medical students, around one mother in ten died of a fever after giving birth. In the second, run by midwives, the death rate was far lower. Women in the city knew this so well that some begged not to be admitted to the first clinic. A young Hungarian doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis, set out to discover why. He examined every difference he could think of, from the position in which women gave birth to the route the priest took through the wards, and found nothing. Then, in 1847, a colleague died after cutting his finger during a post-mortem examination, and his symptoms were strikingly similar to those of the dying mothers. Semmelweis hypothesised that the doctors themselves were carrying "cadaverous particles" from the bodies they examined in the morning to the women they treated afterwards. The midwives, by contrast, did not perform post-mortems. He ordered all staff to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients. The results were dramatic: within months, the death rate in the first clinic fell to around one or two per cent. One might expect that Semmelweis was celebrated. Instead, many senior doctors rejected his conclusions. Some were offended by the suggestion that they were responsible for their patients' deaths; others objected that he could not explain the mechanism behind his findings. Semmelweis did not help his case: he was slow to publish and often attacked his critics angrily. He died in 1865, and it was not until germ theory was established in the following decades that his ideas were widely accepted. Today, his story is a reminder that robust evidence is not always enough. Science depends not only on data but also on people who are willing to accept uncomfortable conclusions.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. We've all suffered through a boring presentation. Dr Reem Khalil trains people in public speaking. Reem, why are so many presentations so dull?
Mostly because people put too much on their slides and then read them aloud. If the audience can read your slide, they don't need you.
So what's the alternative?

One fun format is called Pecha Kucha. It was invented in Tokyo in 2003 by two architects who were tired of long, rambling presentations. The rules are simple: twenty slides, and each slide shows for exactly twenty seconds. The whole talk lasts six minutes and forty seconds.
That sounds stressful!

It forces you to be clear. You can't waffle, because the slide moves on whether you're ready or not. Another useful guide comes from the businessman Guy Kawasaki: no more than ten slides, no longer than twenty minutes, and no font smaller than thirty points.
What about nerves?

Everyone gets butterflies. Even experienced speakers do. The trick is to practise out loud, not just in your head, and to do a dry run in the real room if you can. And remember: the audience wants you to succeed. They're on your side.
One final tip?
Know your first sentence and your last sentence by heart. If you start strong and finish strong, people will forgive almost anything in the middle.

reading.text: How long does it take to form a first impression? According to a well-known series of experiments carried out at Princeton University in 2006, the answer is about one tenth of a second. The psychologists Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed volunteers photographs of unfamiliar faces for different lengths of time and asked them to judge qualities such as trustworthiness and competence. Judgements made after just a hundred milliseconds were remarkably similar to those made by people who had looked at the same faces for as long as they liked. Longer exposure did not change people's opinions very much; it simply made them more confident. Earlier research had already suggested how powerful such "thin slices" of behaviour can be. In the early 1990s, the psychologists Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal showed students short silent video clips of university teachers they had never met. Ratings based on clips lasting only a few seconds were strongly linked to the evaluations given by the teachers' own students at the end of a whole semester. For anyone preparing for an interview, these findings might sound alarming. If judgements are made in an instant, what is the point of preparing detailed answers? Yet there is a second, more encouraging, side to the research. First impressions are fast, but they are not always accurate, and many employers are aware of this. Large reviews of research on recruitment have found that structured interviews, in which every candidate is asked the same carefully designed questions, predict job performance far better than informal conversations. Many organisations now use them precisely because they reduce the influence of snap judgements. The practical lesson is twofold. Candidates should take first impressions seriously: a warm greeting, steady eye contact and a calm voice all help. But they need not despair if they get off to a nervous start. In a well-designed interview, what you say still matters a great deal.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. Have you ever said "yes" and been misunderstood? Dr Nadia Kamal trains business people to work across cultures. Nadia, where should we start?

With the anthropologist Edward T. Hall. In 1976, he introduced the idea of high-context and low-context cultures. In low-context cultures, such as Germany or the United States, people say exactly what they mean. In high-context cultures, such as Japan or most of the Arab world, a lot of the meaning is in the situation, the relationship and what is left unsaid.
Can you give an example?

Imagine an Iraqi manager tells a German colleague, "We'll see, it might be difficult." The German may think the answer is still open. The Iraqi manager probably means "no", but politely. Neither of them is wrong; they're using different codes.
So it's about directness?

Partly. The business writer Erin Meyer, in her book The Culture Map, describes eight scales on which cultures differ, including how people give negative feedback, how they make decisions and how they build trust. Some cultures build trust through tasks: you do good work, so I trust you. Others build it through relationships: we share a meal, so we can work together.
Isn't there a risk of stereotyping?

Absolutely. These scales describe general tendencies, not individuals. There are direct Iraqis and indirect Germans! The real skill is cultural intelligence: noticing differences, staying curious and adapting without losing yourself.

reading.text: Every culture has its unwritten rules: how close to stand, when to arrive, how to say no. Most of us learn our own rules so early that we are hardly aware of them; we notice them only when someone breaks them. A visitor who refuses a second cup of tea in an Iraqi home, or who arrives exactly on time for a dinner party in a country where guests are expected to be late, may cause offence without having the slightest idea why. In the 1970s, the Dutch psychologist Geert Hofstede analysed surveys of employees working for the same multinational company in dozens of countries. He identified several dimensions along which national cultures seemed to differ: how much people accept unequal power, whether they see themselves mainly as individuals or as members of groups, and how comfortable they are with uncertainty. His work became enormously influential in business schools – and enormously controversial. Critics argued that national averages say little about any particular person, and that cultures change over time. In the early 2000s, researchers Christopher Earley and Soon Ang proposed a different approach. Instead of memorising lists of facts about other cultures, they argued, people should develop cultural intelligence: a general ability to work effectively with people from any background. Cultural intelligence, in their view, has several parts: knowledge about how cultures differ; the motivation to engage with people who are different; the ability to adjust your behaviour; and the habit of reflecting on your own assumptions. Crucially, they claimed, it can be learned. This shift matters. Facts about other countries quickly go out of date, and they encourage stereotypes. Curiosity, humility and attention, on the other hand, work everywhere. The culturally intelligent person does not know every custom; instead, they notice when something has gone wrong, ask instead of assuming, and adjust. In an interconnected world, that may be one of the most valuable skills a person can have.

lines.s: Welcome to The Thinking Room. You've probably heard of the "10,000-hour rule": practise anything for ten thousand hours and you'll become an expert. Is it true? Dr Haider Aziz studies expertise.

The idea comes from research by the psychologist Anders Ericsson. In 1993, he and his colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The best students had practised, on average, around ten thousand hours by the age of twenty, far more than the less successful ones.
So the rule is correct?

Not exactly. The writer Malcolm Gladwell made the number famous in his 2008 book Outliers, but Ericsson himself said that it had been misunderstood. There's nothing magic about ten thousand. Some skills take far less; others take far more. And, crucially, the type of practice matters more than the number of hours.
What kind of practice?

Ericsson called it deliberate practice. It means working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of your ability, with clear goals and immediate feedback, ideally from a teacher. Simply repeating what you can already do doesn't count.
Does talent matter at all?

That's hotly debated. A large review in 2014 found that deliberate practice explained a significant part of the differences between people in games and music, but a much smaller part in education and professions. So practice matters a lot, but it isn't the whole story.
What does that mean for language learners?
Don't just spend hours with English; spend them wisely. Find your weaknesses, focus on them, and get feedback. An hour of deliberate practice is worth a week of passive listening.

reading.text: Two of the most successful sportsmen of recent decades followed strikingly different paths. The golfer Tiger Woods famously began practising before he was two years old and was trained intensively in a single sport throughout his childhood. The tennis player Roger Federer, by contrast, tried a wide range of sports as a boy, including football, skiing, basketball and badminton, and only began to focus seriously on tennis in his teens. Both became among the greatest players in history. So which approach is better? For years, the popular answer was clear: start early and specialise. In his book Range, published in 2019, the writer David Epstein challenged this assumption. He argued that early specialisation works well in what psychologists call "kind" learning environments, where the rules are clear, patterns repeat and feedback is quick and accurate. Golf and chess are good examples. In these fields, deliberate practice from an early age can produce extraordinary results. Most of life, however, is not like this. In "wicked" learning environments, the rules are unclear or change over time, feedback is delayed or misleading, and problems rarely repeat themselves exactly. Epstein suggested that in such environments, which include business, science and many creative fields, generalists often have an advantage. People who have sampled many areas tend to be better at transferring knowledge from one field to another, at recognising patterns that specialists miss and at adapting when circumstances change. This does not mean that expertise is unimportant. Rather, it suggests that the path to expertise need not be narrow. A period of exploration, far from being a waste of time, may help people discover where their real strengths lie. For language learners, the lesson is encouraging. Every book you read, every film you watch and every subject you study in English, however unrelated it may seem, adds to the range from which your mastery will eventually grow.

lines.s: For our final episode, we're asking a big question: who does English belong to? Professor Laila Hassan is a sociolinguist. Laila, welcome.
Thank you. It's a pleasure to be here for the final episode!
Let's start with numbers. How many people speak English?
Estimates vary, but the linguist David Crystal has suggested that well over a billion people use English, and that non-native speakers now outnumber native speakers by roughly three or four to one.
So most English conversations don't include a native speaker at all?

Very often, yes. When an Iraqi engineer talks to a Korean client, or a Brazilian student emails a professor in Germany, English is a shared tool that belongs to both of them. In 1985, the linguist Braj Kachru described English in three circles: an inner circle, like Britain and the United States; an outer circle, like India and Nigeria, where English has an official role; and an expanding circle, like Iraq, China or Brazil, where it's learned as a foreign language.
Does that mean learners should stop trying to sound British or American?

It means the goal has changed. The aim isn't to erase your accent; it's intelligibility, flexibility and confidence. Many of the most effective international communicators have clear accents from their first language.
Any final advice for listeners who've just finished a C1 course?

Stop thinking of yourself as a learner of someone else's language. At C1, English is your language too. Use it to read, to argue, to create and to connect. The real test isn't an exam; it's what you do with English next.

reading.text: More than six hundred years ago, the scholar Ibn Khaldun, writing in North Africa, described how people acquire language with remarkable insight. In his famous Muqaddimah, he argued that a language is not simply a collection of rules to be memorised, but a malaka, an acquired habit or skill that becomes firmly established through constant practice. Just as a carpenter does not become skilled by reading about wood, he suggested, a speaker does not master a language by studying grammar alone. Mastery comes from repeated exposure to good examples and from using the language until it becomes second nature. Ibn Khaldun even observed that some scholars who knew every rule of Arabic grammar could not write an elegant letter, while others who had memorised and imitated fine poetry and prose wrote beautifully without being able to explain the rules at all. Knowledge about a language, in other words, is not the same as the ability to use it. Modern research would largely agree. Linguists today distinguish between explicit knowledge, which we can describe, and implicit knowledge, which we use automatically without thinking. Studies of language learning suggest that the second develops mainly through large amounts of meaningful input and output: reading, listening, speaking and writing about things that matter to us. Grammar instruction still has an important role, helping learners to notice patterns they might otherwise miss, but it works best when it supports real use rather than replacing it. If you have reached the end of this book, you have done exactly what Ibn Khaldun recommended. You have read hundreds of texts, written dozens of essays, listened to sixty episodes and practised the same structures again and again until they began to feel natural. The habit is now yours. What remains is to keep using it: to read widely, to write often and to speak without fear. Mastery, as Ibn Khaldun understood, is not a destination but a way of life.
